title: The Pharisee Thanked God He Was Better Than Everyone Else — Jesus Wasn’t Impressed
paragraphs: The Pharisee Thanked God He Was Better Than Everyone Else — Jesus Wasn’t Impressed
He prayed. He fasted. He gave. He lived cleaner than the man standing behind him. And somehow, the sinner walked home right with God… while the religious man did not.
There is a kind of prayer that sounds holy enough to survive in church…
but reveals a heart frighteningly far from grace.
Jesus once told a story about two men who walked into the same temple.
Both believed in God.
Both prayed.
Both stood in a place associated with worship.
But only one walked away justified.
And the disturbing part is that, if you had been standing outside the temple judging them by reputation, religious discipline, and visible morality…
you might have picked the wrong man.
Jesus introduced the parable with a warning that should make every serious Christian examine his or her heart:
“He spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others.” — Luke 18:9, KJV
That sentence exposes the disease before Jesus even introduces the patients.
They trusted in themselves.
The Greek expression is πεποιθότας ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς (pepoithotas eph’ heautois)—people who had placed their confidence in themselves.
And that confidence produced something else.
They “despised others.”
The Greek verb is ἐξουθενέω (exoutheneō), carrying the idea of treating someone as insignificant, contemptible, or of no account.
That is where self-righteousness eventually takes you.
First, you become impressed with yourself.
Then you become less impressed with everyone else.
And eventually, while speaking respectfully about God, you can begin looking down upon the very people He came to save.
Jesus continued:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.” — Luke 18:10, KJV
A Pharisee.
And a tax collector.
To modern ears, “Pharisee” can automatically sound like the villain because we already know so many Gospel stories. But Jesus’ original audience did not have the luxury of reading the ending first.
The Pharisee represented visible religious seriousness.
The tax collector represented scandal.
Tax collectors were widely despised because of their association with Rome and the opportunities their profession created for exploitation and corruption.
So imagine these two men walking toward the temple.
One has a religious résumé.
The other carries a reputation.
One probably expects respect.
The other has reasons to feel ashamed.
Then the Pharisee begins praying.
And at first…
his prayer actually sounds like thanksgiving.
“God, I thank thee…”
What could possibly be wrong with thanking God?
Nothing.
Until you hear what he is thankful for.
“God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are…”
There it is.
The prayer has barely begun, and another human being has already become the measuring stick.
He continues:
“…extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.”
Even this tax collector.
Can you feel the distance in those words?
He is standing before the Holy One…
yet somehow his attention is still on the sinner standing nearby.
That is one of the terrifying characteristics of spiritual pride.
You can become so occupied with somebody else’s sin that you stop trembling over your own need for mercy.
You can know enough Bible to correct everybody…
and still need God to correct you.
You can avoid adultery and secretly feed arrogance.
You can reject drunkenness and become intoxicated with your own reputation.
You can condemn greed while craving recognition.
You can expose somebody’s scandal while hiding your pride behind religious language.
You can even thank God…
while essentially congratulating yourself.
The Pharisee continues:
“I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.” — Luke 18:12, KJV
Notice what dominates the prayer.
I.
I fast.
I give.
I am not like them.
His disciplines were not necessarily the problem.
Fasting can be beautiful.
Giving can be worship.
Moral obedience matters.
Jesus was not teaching that righteousness is evil or that sin does not matter.
The problem was where this man had placed his confidence.
His obedience had become evidence for the prosecution against everyone else.
His spiritual disciplines had become mirrors in which he admired himself.
And somewhere along the way, gratitude for grace had mutated into confidence in religious performance.
That danger did not die with the Pharisees.
It can happen to us.
It can happen to the Christian who has been saved for thirty years and cannot remember what it felt like to desperately need mercy.
It can happen to the Bible teacher who knows Greek words but has forgotten how to weep.
It can happen to the worship leader.
The pastor.
The ministry volunteer.
The Christian content creator.
The person sharing Scripture every morning.
The person reading this article.
It can happen when you see someone’s divorce and quietly think, My marriage would never become that.
When somebody’s child rebels and something inside whispers, They obviously did something wrong.
When another believer falls publicly and your first emotion is satisfaction rather than grief.
When you see an addict, prisoner, prostitute, adulterer, alcoholic, unbeliever, backslider, or struggling Christian…
and forget that apart from grace, you have nothing to boast about.
Paul destroys that illusion with one question:
“For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” — 1 Corinthians 4:7, KJV
What do you possess that you did not ultimately receive?
Breath.
Strength.
Opportunity.
Knowledge.
Forgiveness.
Salvation.
Grace.
If everything good becomes an occasion for gratitude, what remains for boasting?
Nothing.
Then Jesus moves our attention away from the religious man.
There is another man in the temple.
The scandalous one.
The tax collector.
And he does not seem interested in comparing himself with anybody.
“And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven…”
He stands at a distance.
His eyes remain lowered.
Then his body begins preaching what his mouth can barely express.
He “smote upon his breast.”
And finally the prayer comes out.
Seven words in the KJV:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
In Greek:
Ὁ Θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
He brings no résumé.
No comparison.
No list of religious achievements.
No explanation about his childhood.
No reminder that somebody else is worse.
He does not say, “God, at least I am not like that Pharisee.”
Because the moment the tax collector says that…
he becomes another version of the Pharisee.
Instead, there is only confession.
Need.
Mercy.
“God…”
That is where hope begins.
“Be merciful…”
That is what he cannot provide for himself.
“To me…”
No hiding in the sins of other people.
“The sinner.”
No defense.
And then Jesus says something that must have shocked His listeners:
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other…” — Luke 18:14, KJV
Read that again.
The tax collector went home justified.
The Greek word is δεδικαιωμένος (dedikaiōmenos), from δικαιόω (dikaioō), meaning to justify or declare righteous.
The scandalous man did not walk home justified because his sin suddenly became harmless.
He walked home justified because he stopped pretending he could make himself righteous before God.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not God announcing that sin does not matter.
Look at the cross and try to say sin does not matter.
The cross tells us precisely how serious sin is.
The sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.” — Romans 4:25, KJV
Christianity is not the story of decent people proving they deserve heaven.
It is the story of guilty people being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel humiliates human pride before it heals the human heart.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
All.
The scandalous sinner.
The respectable sinner.
The obvious sinner.
The religious sinner.
You.
Me.
And that is why comparing ourselves with other people is such a dangerous spiritual game.
God's standard is not your neighbor.
It is not the person whose marriage collapsed.
It is not the unbeliever on Facebook.
It is not the Christian caught in scandal.
It is not the person who drinks more, curses more, knows less Scripture, attends church less, or has made more publicly embarrassing decisions than you.
We have all fallen short of the glory of God.
And if that were the end of the story, there would be no Gospel.
But Paul continues.
We are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:24, KJV
Freely.
By grace.
Through redemption.
In Christ Jesus.
That is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody discovered what you watched.
What you thought.
What you wanted.
What you almost did.
Maybe your greatest sin has always worn respectable clothes.
Maybe your addiction was approval.
Maybe your idol was reputation.
Maybe your secret pleasure was being considered more spiritual than other people.
Maybe you never said, “God, thank You that I am better than them.”
You just felt it.
And perhaps that is why this parable hurts.
Because sometimes the Pharisee is not standing across the room.
Sometimes he is standing inside us.
Self-righteousness rarely introduces itself as self-righteousness.
It calls itself discernment.
Standards.
Conviction.
Being “biblical.”
And yes, Christians absolutely need discernment, standards, conviction, and biblical truth.
But biblical conviction should make us hate sin without teaching us to hate sinners.
Truth without grace becomes a weapon.
Grace without truth becomes sentimentality.
Jesus embodies both perfectly.
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us… full of grace and truth.” — John 1:14, KJV
Grace and truth.
Jesus does not save us by pretending darkness is light.
He enters our darkness and calls us into His light.
He does not tell the guilty, “You were righteous all along.”
He offers something infinitely better.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new life.
Himself.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is the sinner finally abandoning the courtroom speech.
No more excuses.
No more comparison.
No more hiding behind somebody worse.
No more pointing across the temple.
Just:
“God, be merciful to me.”
And because of Jesus Christ, mercy is not wishful thinking.
There is a cross.
There is blood shed for the forgiveness of sins.
There is an empty tomb.
There is a living Savior.
There is grace for the guilty.
John writes:
Notice something astonishing.
Faithful and just.
At the cross, forgiveness is not God becoming careless about justice.
Christ bore our sins.
Our hope rests not in pretending guilt away, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the most important question after reading Luke 18 is not:
“Who are the Pharisees I know?”
That question is dangerously easy.
Try another one.
Where is the Pharisee in me?
Who have you secretly decided is beneath you?
Whose failure makes you feel better about yourself?
Whose scandal have you repeated more eagerly than you have prayed for their restoration?
Whose sin disgusts you while your own pride barely troubles you?
Who have you mentally placed at the back of the temple while quietly assuming God must be impressed that you are standing near the front?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If God is exposing pride, do not defend it.
Bring it into the light.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need grace is one small way of refusing to keep pretending.
And please understand this: the answer to religious pride is not to become proud of being “less religious.”
The tax collector would miss the entire point if he walked outside saying, “Thank God I’m not like that Pharisee.”
The answer is Jesus.
Always Jesus.
His righteousness instead of our boasting.
His mercy instead of our merit.
His cross instead of our résumé.
His resurrection instead of our hopelessness.
His glory instead of ours.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
And the next verse reminds us that grace does not leave us unchanged:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” — Ephesians 2:10, KJV
Saved not by good works.
Saved for good works.
Grace does not produce spiritual laziness.
Real grace transforms people.
We obey not to purchase the love of God, but because in Christ we have encountered a love we could never purchase.
So tonight, before you tell God about everybody who needs fixing…
ask Him to search you.
Before sharing another person's scandal…
remember your Savior.
Before celebrating that you did not fall where somebody else fell…
remember Who has been holding you upright.
And when someone does fall, do not confuse compassion with approval of sin.
Speak truth.
Call sin what Scripture calls it.
But speak as somebody who knows what it costs to be forgiven.
Galatians 6:1 tells spiritual believers to restore someone overtaken in a fault “in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.”
That is Gospel restoration.
Not compromise.
Not superiority.
Truth kneeling beside grace.
Return to it the next time spiritual pride whispers that somebody else’s failure makes you righteous.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks failure has placed them beyond Christ's mercy.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor.
Let support flow from gratitude to God—not pressure, spiritual pride, or fear.
But never forget why any of this exists.
Not to build our name.
Not to create another religious club where respectable people congratulate themselves for being better than everybody outside.
Not to produce modern Pharisees with Christian merchandise and Bible verses in their bios.
We exist to point sinners to Jesus.
And that includes us.
The Pharisee entered the temple carrying his accomplishments.
The tax collector entered carrying his guilt.
One told God why he was impressive.
The other begged God for mercy.
And Jesus said the broken man went home justified.
That is scandalous grace.
The Gospel does not tell you to become impressive enough that God finally notices you.
It tells you that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
So come down from the pedestal.
Drop the résumé.
Stop comparing scars.
Stop keeping score.
Stop trying to make another person's darkness prove that you are standing in the light.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
And then rise—not boasting that you are better than everyone else, but amazed that Christ was willing to save you at all.
Because one day, when every earthly reputation has disappeared and every hidden motive stands exposed, there will be only one righteousness strong enough to carry a sinner home.
Not yours.
His.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after you close this article:
The moment you stop needing to be better than the sinner beside you may be the moment you finally understand why both of you need the Savior.
